7. A Chinook salmon can jump out of water with a speed v0 and an angle 𝜃 above the horizontal. What is the speed of the fish when it is at the maximum height?
A. 𝑣0.
B. 𝑣0 cos 𝜃.
C. 𝑣0 sin 𝜃.
D. 0.
datasource_item.generated_question_text:
Q7. A soccer ball is kicked with a speed v_0 at an angle θ above the horizontal. What is the speed of the ball when it is at the maximum height? (Neglect air resistance.)
A. v_0.
The speed is not generally the launch speed because the vertical component decreases to zero at the top.
B. v_0 cos θ.
At maximum height the vertical velocity is zero while the horizontal component remains v_0 cos θ, so the speed equals v_0 cos θ.
C. v_0 sin θ.
This is the initial vertical component, but at maximum height the vertical component is zero.
D. 0.
Only the vertical component becomes zero at the top; the horizontal component generally remains nonzero.

10. An object can escape a planet with radius R and mass M at an escape speed given by 𝑣 = √2𝐺𝑀⁄𝑅, where 𝐺 is the universal gravitational constant. Based on this expression for escape speed, which of the following statements is correct?
A. A heavier object requires a higher speed to escape from the planet.
B. A lighter object requires a lower speed to escape from the planet.
C. An object requires a higher speed to escape from a planet with smaller mass and a larger radius.
D. An object requires a higher speed to escape from a planet with greater mass and a smaller radius.
datasource_item.generated_question_text:
Q10. A probe can escape a celestial body of radius R and mass M at an escape speed given by v = \sqrt{2GM/R}, where G is the universal gravitational constant. Based on this expression for escape speed, which of the following statements is correct?
A. A more massive probe requires a higher speed to escape from the same body.
The probe’s mass does not appear in v = \sqrt{2GM/R}, so escape speed is independent of the escaping object’s mass.
B. A less massive probe requires a lower speed to escape from the same body.

A. It stays the same.

B. It decreases by a factor of 4.
Since F ∝ q_1q_2/r^2, doubling both charges gives a factor of 4 while increasing distance by 4 gives a factor of 16 in the denominator, so F becomes 4/16 = 1/4 of the original.
C. It increases by a factor of 4.
This accounts for doubling charges but forgets that increasing separation reduces force by the square of the distance factor.
D. It increases by a factor of 16.
This incorrectly treats the distance change as increasing the force rather than decreasing it via r^2.
E. It decreases by a factor of 2.
This is a common arithmetic slip that does not correctly combine the ×4 charge effect with the ÷16 distance-squared effect.

11. The force 𝐹⃗ = (3.04N)𝑖̂ + (4.01N)𝑗̂. acts on a particle as it moves along the x axis from x = 0.33 m to x = 5.03 m. What is the work, in joules, done by the force on the particle?
A. 20.5 J
B. 14.3 J
C. 5.00 J
D. 35.7 J
datasource_item.generated_question_text:
Q11. The force \vec{F} = (-2.50\ \mathrm{N})\hat{i} + (6.00\ \mathrm{N})\hat{j} acts on a particle as it moves along the y axis from y = 1.20 m to y = 4.70 m. What is the work, in joules, done by the force on the particle?
A. 21.0 J.
The displacement is \Delta\vec{r} = (3.50\ \mathrm{m})\hat{j}, so W = \vec{F} · \Delta\vec{r} = (6.00)(3.50) = 21.0 J.
B. −8.75 J.
This incorrectly uses the x-component of force even though the displacement is purely along y.
C. 8.75 J.
This takes the magnitude of the x-component contribution, but there is no x-displacement so the x-force does no work.
D. 27.5 J.
This commonly comes from using the force magnitude times distance instead of the dot product with the correct direction.
